name: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)
tagline: Show me who your neighbours are, and I will tell you who you are.
introduction: K-Nearest Neighbours is an intuitive instance-based, non-parametric, 'lazy learning' algorithm. It does not learn an explicit mathematical model during training; instead, it stores the training dataset. When predicting a new sample, it computes the distance between that sample and all stored training points, identifies the K closest neighbours, and assigns the majority class (or average value).
why_used: Extremely simple conceptual foundation requiring zero mathematical assumptions about underlying probability distributions.
No training phase (O(1) training time) makes it immediately ready to ingest new training examples.
Adapts flexibly to complex, irregular decision boundaries that linear boundaries cannot separate.
how_it_works:
1. Store the training feature matrix and labels.
2. For an unseen query point, compute its distance to every point in the training set using a distance metric (e.g. Euclidean, Manhattan).
3. Sort the distances and select the top K closest points.
4. For classification: take the majority vote among the K neighbours.
5. For regression: calculate the mean (or distance-weighted mean) of the K target values.
mathematical_intuition: KNN assumes that points close to each other in feature space share similar outcomes. The choice of K acts as a direct knob for model bias and variance: small K (e.g., K=1) creates complex, highly wiggly decision boundaries sensitive to noise (low bias, high variance); large K smooths out boundaries (high bias, low variance).

important_formulas.name: Euclidean Distance (L2 Norm)
important_formulas.description: Straight-line geometric distance between two vectors in n-dimensional Euclidean space.

important_formulas.name: Manhattan Distance (L1 Norm / City Block)
important_formulas.description: Sum of absolute differences along each feature axis; more robust to extreme outlier values.

important_formulas.name: Minkowski Distance (Generalized)
important_formulas.description: General distance metric where p=1 yields Manhattan and p=2 yields Euclidean.

step_by_step_example.scenario: Classifying a new point X = (3, 4) with K=3 using Euclidean distance.
step_by_step_example.top_k_neighbors: Closest 3: Point A (1.41, Class 0), Point B (1.41, Class 1), Point C (2.0, Class 1)
step_by_step_example.conclusion: Query point is classified as Class 1 by majority vote (2/3).

advantages: Zero training cost: simply stores points in memory.
Highly intuitive logic: easily explained to beginners through spatial closeness.
Can model arbitrary non-linear multi-class boundaries naturally.
New training observations can be added incrementally without retraining from scratch.
disadvantages: Expensive test-time prediction: computing distances against N samples scales as O(N * D).
Curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions, distance metrics collapse as all points become equidistant.
Sensitive to feature scaling: features with large numerical magnitudes completely dominate the distance metric.
Sensitive to irrelevant features and noisy labels in dense regions.
when_to_use: Small to medium datasets (less than 10,000 samples).
When features are already scaled or measured in uniform physical units.
When quick prototyping without parameter tuning is desired.
when_to_avoid: High-dimensional data (e.g., text document vectors with thousands of columns).
Large-scale production systems requiring low-latency real-time inference.
Datasets with unscaled features or severe class imbalance.

comparison_with_related.difference: Logistic Regression is parametric and learns a fixed linear hyperplane during training; KNN is non-parametric and delays all work until prediction time.
Decision Trees make axis-aligned splits ignoring point distances; KNN makes local spherical/elliptical neighborhood predictions.

practical_example: Recommender systems finding users with similar movie watch histories based on cosine or Euclidean similarity.
